preamble: Affrication of the voiced palatal stop [ɟ] to the postalveolar affricate [dʒ]: the large palatal contact is fronted and released with frication. Arabic jīm is the best-known case: Proto-Semitic *g had become palatal [ɟ] or [ɡʲ] by the time of the Quran and then [dʒ], the pronunciation of the Arabian Peninsula, Iraq and Modern Standard Arabic, while other dialects went on to [ʒ] or kept [ɟ]. In Northeastern Gheg Albanian (Kosovo and adjacent areas) standard /ɟ/ ⟨gj⟩ is realized [dʒ], merging with ⟨xh⟩, and Western Friulian has [dʒ] where Central Friulian keeps the palatal stop [ɟ] ⟨gj⟩ from Latin g before a. Found in three unrelated families.

examples.note: Hebrew gāmāl and Egyptian Arabic gamal keep the stop; South Levantine and most Maghrebi dialects continue to ʒamal.
The palatal stops /c ɟ/ ⟨q gj⟩ are realized as [tʃ dʒ], merging with ⟨ç xh⟩.
Central [c ɟ] ⟨cj gj⟩ from Latin c, g before a correspond to Western [tʃ dʒ].

sources: Watson, J. C. E. (2002). The Phonology and Morphology of Arabic. Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780199257591.001.0001
